## Course Title
Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change

## Learning Objectives
- Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0
- Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters
- Describe flood insurance coverage for basements, along with applicable exclusions
- Explain how the NFIP has historically evolved through various legislative changes and how Risk Rating 2.0 was designed to tackle the financial disparities of the program
- Discuss the proposed methods for improving flood insurance affordability
- Describe the impact of climate change on flood risks, the NFIP, private flood insurers, urban areas, and under-resourced communities; and
- Discuss the full scope of the NFIP claims process from pre-flood preparation to post-flood cleanup, as well as the role of adjusters

## Content Sample

[Heading 1] Introduction
Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course!

[Heading 1] 1.0 Coverage, Limits, and Rates
Before we jump into the core content, let’s take a moment to review the basics of NFIP coverage, limits, and rates.

[Heading 2] 1.1 Coverage
Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program.

[Heading 2] 1.2 Coverage Limits
To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn.

[Heading 2] 1.3 Rates
As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past.

[Heading 3] Knowledge Check
Aisha has flood insurance on her single-family home with a $2,000 deductible for building coverage and a $1,000 deductible for contents coverage. When her home and personal property are damaged in a covered flood event, how much is Aisha responsible for paying before her flood insurance will kick in? (Refer to Section 1.1, Page 8)

[Heading 1] 2.0 Upping Your NFIP Insurance Game
Now that you have a basic understanding of how flood insurance works in terms of coverage, limits, and rates, it’s time to up your NFIP insurance game and examine how these factors extend to communities that are often overlooked as susceptible to flooding: urban areas.

[Heading 2] 2.1 Coverage for Floods in Urban Areas
Some people believe floods do not pose a risk to urban areas. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system.

[Heading 3] 2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance
Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion.

## Course Title
Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change

## Learning Objectives
- Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0
- Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters
- Describe flood insurance coverage for basements, along with applicable exclusions
- Explain how the NFIP has historically evolved through various legislative changes and how Risk Rating 2.0 was designed to tackle the financial disparities of the program
- Discuss the proposed methods for improving flood insurance affordability
- Describe the impact of climate change on flood risks, the NFIP, private flood insurers, urban areas, and under-resourced communities; and
- Discuss the full scope of the NFIP claims process from pre-flood preparation to post-flood cleanup, as well as the role of adjusters

## Content Sample

[Heading 1] Introduction
Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course!

[Heading 1] 1.0 Coverage, Limits, and Rates
Before we jump into the core content, let’s take a moment to review the basics of NFIP coverage, limits, and rates.

[Heading 2] 1.1 Coverage
Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program.

[Heading 2] 1.2 Coverage Limits
To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn.

[Heading 2] 1.3 Rates
As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past.

[Heading 3] Knowledge Check
Aisha has flood insurance on her single-family home with a $2,000 deductible for building coverage and a $1,000 deductible for contents coverage. When her home and personal property are damaged in a covered flood event, how much is Aisha responsible for paying before her flood insurance will kick in? (Refer to Section 1.1, Page 8)

[Heading 1] 2.0 Upping Your NFIP Insurance Game
Now that you have a basic understanding of how flood insurance works in terms of coverage, limits, and rates, it’s time to up your NFIP insurance game and examine how these factors extend to communities that are often overlooked as susceptible to flooding: urban areas.

[Heading 2] 2.1 Coverage for Floods in Urban Areas
Some people believe floods do not pose a risk to urban areas. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system.

[Heading 3] 2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance
Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion.

## Course Title

## Learning Objectives
- Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0
- Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters

## Content Sample

[Heading 1] Introduction
Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course!

[Heading 1] 1.0 Coverage, Limits, and Rates
Before we jump into the core content, let’s take a moment to review the basics of NFIP coverage, limits, and rates.

[Heading 2] 1.1 Coverage
Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program.

[Heading 2] 1.2 Coverage Limits
To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn.

[Heading 2] 1.3 Rates
As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past.

[Heading 3] Knowledge Check
Aisha has flood insurance on her single-family home with a $2,000 deductible for building coverage and a $1,000 deductible for contents coverage. When her home and personal property are damaged in a covered flood event, how much is Aisha responsible for paying before her flood insurance will kick in? (Refer to Section 1.1, Page 8)

[Heading 1] 2.0 Upping Your NFIP Insurance Game
Now that you have a basic understanding of how flood insurance works in terms of coverage, limits, and rates, it’s time to up your NFIP insurance game and examine how these factors extend to communities that are often overlooked as susceptible to flooding: urban areas.

[Heading 2] 2.1 Coverage for Floods in Urban Areas
Some people believe floods do not pose a risk to urban areas. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system.

[Heading 3] 2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance
Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion.

## Course Title
Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change

## Learning Objectives
- Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0
- Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters
- Describe flood insurance coverage for basements, along with applicable exclusions
- Explain how the NFIP has historically evolved through various legislative changes and how Risk Rating 2.0 was designed to tackle the financial disparities of the program
- Discuss the proposed methods for improving flood insurance affordability
- Describe the impact of climate change on flood risks, the NFIP, private flood insurers, urban areas, and under-resourced communities; and
- Discuss the full scope of the NFIP claims process from pre-flood preparation to post-flood cleanup, as well as the role of adjusters

## Content Sample

[Heading 1] Introduction
Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course!

[Heading 1] 1.0 Coverage, Limits, and Rates
Before we jump into the core content, let’s take a moment to review the basics of NFIP coverage, limits, and rates.

[Heading 2] 1.1 Coverage
Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program.

[Heading 2] 1.2 Coverage Limits
To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn.

[Heading 2] 1.3 Rates
As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past.

[Heading 3] Knowledge Check
Aisha has flood insurance on her single-family home with a $2,000 deductible for building coverage and a $1,000 deductible for contents coverage. When her home and personal property are damaged in a covered flood event, how much is Aisha responsible for paying before her flood insurance will kick in? (Refer to Section 1.1, Page 8)

[Heading 1] 2.0 Upping Your NFIP Insurance Game
Now that you have a basic understanding of how flood insurance works in terms of coverage, limits, and rates, it’s time to up your NFIP insurance game and examine how these factors extend to communities that are often overlooked as susceptible to flooding: urban areas.

[Heading 2] 2.1 Coverage for Floods in Urban Areas
Some people believe floods do not pose a risk to urban areas. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system.

[Heading 3] 2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance
Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion.

## Course Title

## Learning Objectives
- Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0
- Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters
- Describe flood insurance coverage for basements, along with applicable exclusions

## Content Sample

[Heading 1] Introduction
Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course!

[Heading 1] 1.0 Coverage, Limits, and Rates
Before we jump into the core content, let’s take a moment to review the basics of NFIP coverage, limits, and rates.

[Heading 2] 1.1 Coverage
Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program.

[Heading 2] 1.2 Coverage Limits
To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn.

[Heading 2] 1.3 Rates
As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past.

[Heading 3] Knowledge Check
Aisha has flood insurance on her single-family home with a $2,000 deductible for building coverage and a $1,000 deductible for contents coverage. When her home and personal property are damaged in a covered flood event, how much is Aisha responsible for paying before her flood insurance will kick in? (Refer to Section 1.1, Page 8)

[Heading 1] 2.0 Upping Your NFIP Insurance Game
Now that you have a basic understanding of how flood insurance works in terms of coverage, limits, and rates, it’s time to up your NFIP insurance game and examine how these factors extend to communities that are often overlooked as susceptible to flooding: urban areas.

[Heading 2] 2.1 Coverage for Floods in Urban Areas
Some people believe floods do not pose a risk to urban areas. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system.

[Heading 3] 2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance
Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion.

## Course Title
Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change

## Learning Objectives
- Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0
- Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters
- Describe flood insurance coverage for basements, along with applicable exclusions
- Explain how the NFIP has historically evolved through various legislative changes and how Risk Rating 2.0 was designed to tackle the financial disparities of the program
- Discuss the proposed methods for improving flood insurance affordability
- Describe the impact of climate change on flood risks, the NFIP, private flood insurers, urban areas, and under-resourced communities; and
- Discuss the full scope of the NFIP claims process from pre-flood preparation to post-flood cleanup, as well as the role of adjusters

## Content Sample

[Heading 1] Introduction
Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course!

[Heading 1] 1.0 Coverage, Limits, and Rates
Before we jump into the core content, let’s take a moment to review the basics of NFIP coverage, limits, and rates.

[Heading 2] 1.1 Coverage
Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program.

[Heading 2] 1.2 Coverage Limits
To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn.

[Heading 2] 1.3 Rates
As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past.

[Heading 3] Knowledge Check
Aisha has flood insurance on her single-family home with a $2,000 deductible for building coverage and a $1,000 deductible for contents coverage. When her home and personal property are damaged in a covered flood event, how much is Aisha responsible for paying before her flood insurance will kick in? (Refer to Section 1.1, Page 8)

[Heading 1] 2.0 Upping Your NFIP Insurance Game
Now that you have a basic understanding of how flood insurance works in terms of coverage, limits, and rates, it’s time to up your NFIP insurance game and examine how these factors extend to communities that are often overlooked as susceptible to flooding: urban areas.

[Heading 2] 2.1 Coverage for Floods in Urban Areas
Some people believe floods do not pose a risk to urban areas. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system.

[Heading 3] 2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance
Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion.
